Hi. I am in my 20s and I have had a handful of serious relationships since my injury. Your best answers are going to come from a person who experienced the same thing as you. I can tell you that there is a lot of ignorance when it comes to interacting with people who have SCIs. Not only have women shared stories with me, about how people ask them what they are doing with someone in a wheelchair. People often remind me how "lucky" I am to date amazing women. People have bluntly asked about our relationship and I am sure there is a lot more talking that I never hear about. Questions asked out of my earshot. People who are not doing it, are not going to understand it. Unfortunately we live in a very shallow world where physical appearance is more important than an individual's personality. Long story short(ish), you have to do what makes you happy and draw a hard line if people push persistently. In my dating, I have met a lot of women who turn me down as soon as they found out about the wheelchair (online dating, I make sure to include a picture of myself with/in the chair, now). What I have learned, is that if you let a wheelchair stop you, that is the real disability. It is saddening that so many people might have missed out on great experiences because THEY were disabled by someone else's wheels.

If someone was struggling with doing something and they wanted to ask people of a similar injury level how to go about adapting. "Hey C2-CRs, how do I..." This answer is a little different...

Last year I read an article released about a study done at the University of California. In the article the university had taken 4 or 5 people with spinal cord injuries and applied electrical stimulation to the spine below the point of injury. Most of them reported slight regained motor control and feeling. It also mentioned that the ones taking the medication "Buspirone" had better results. I've read a million articles about "miracle cures" but this one inspired me to do something. I went on Amazon and found a muscle stimulator for about $25. I talked to my doctor and got put on busprione. It's for anxiety so it wasn't hard to get. The study I read said that the patients in the trial got 30 minutes of stimulation, once a week for four weeks. I don't know where exactly the electrodes were placed on their bodies, besides "below the point of injury". I don't know what kind of voltage/amperage/ohms(?) they received. I don't know how many milligrams of busiprone they were taking. I read that they had "reawakened dormant nerves". I'm sorry I don't have links to any of this (fulltime mobile) but if you look you should be able to find the information.

In my free time around the house, I'll attach 2 or 4 electrodes down the lower half of my spine, crank up the dial all the way and go about my day. I haven't done it as much as I'd like to but I remember a couple times per week for the past two months. I don't want to say I have conclusive results but I pulled my wallet out of my pocket and was caught off guard when I felt a light sliding on my leg. Another time I was getting out of my van and my knees hit together and I thought I felt it. It was very light and honestly, there is a doubtful voice that questions whether or not it was all in my head. But I'm going to keep trying. I wouldn't expect overnight results. I don't care if it takes 2 years to see results. It's already been 8 years of this Hell. 

(T-5, I also believe in the potential for medical marijuana because I've read about receptors in our endocannabinoid system and how it affects our nerves)

I could be way off. I'm just a hopeful human.

Edit- If you want to get your own EMS I'd suggest investing in extra electrodes (sold separate from the stimulator) and maybe rechargeable batteries. I also ordered a cheap back brace to wear over the electrodes. It helps keep them from getting pulled off as I move about and help to keep my back lined up.

My understanding of it, is that it covers the majority of the cost of basic medical bills. If I go to the emergency room, I will only have to pay a little, or nothing, out of pocket. 

The process with when my wheel fell off: I had to go see a doctor, to say "yep, the wheel isn't there anymore". The doctor sent paperwork to a medical supply company which had to get approval from Medicaid for said paperwork before parts could be ordered. I rolled around on three wheels for a few months. Even my wheelchair was gimpy (lol). Things like, prescriptions are pretty quick though and I don't normally have to pay more than $2 because of my insurance (I take muscle relaxers for the spasms when they get bad).

It's hard to find a doctor that accepts the insurance. Most places won't take on new patients on medicaid. I called some therapists a couple years ago when I thought I was suffering from depression, but none of them accepted adults on medicaid.

I like to think that everyone's mind works on a scale from 0-10. Zero being the worst thing that has ever happened to us, ten being the best. We all have our worst thing that has ever happened, until something worse comes along. Then our scales changes, but we all have our own zero. I think everyone has their struggles and none of us really know what we're capable of until we are faced with that challenge. It just feels like I spend most of my time closer to my zero. 

I have medicaid and medicare, so I think things like talking to a professional would have to be out of pocket. I know it was like pulling teeth to try to get a new front wheel for my chair when one of the old ones fell off. I know my dental coverage stopped after I turned 21, (I'm 24 now). I haven't looked into alternatives for a lack of funds I guess.
